title: Analysing Routing in a Mixture-of-Experts Model

A footnote on that hit guard
5. What does routing actually depend on?
7. How far does one script get?

segments.html:
📗 You can find an interactive Colab version of this tutorial here.

A mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer replaces a transformer block's single MLP with many parallel MLPs — the experts — and a small linear router that picks a few of them per token. Only the picked experts run, so the model can hold billions of parameters while spending the compute of a much smaller one.

That makes routing an unusually attractive target for interpretability. Unlike a direction in the residual stream, the routing decision is discrete, named and countable: for every token you get a short list of expert ids. It is tempting to read those lists as a map of what the model has specialised in, and to test that map by deleting an expert and watching the loss.

Both halves of that plan have a trap in them, and this tutorial is mostly about the traps. We will:

  1. find the router and work out what its output actually is, without being told;
  2. anchor the reading — check that the experts we think were selected really are the top-k of the logits we read, and that the weights really are the softmax of those logits;
  3. show that the obvious expert ablation — masking a router logit to -inf — is a silent no-op on the transformers backend, understand why, and replace it with one that works;
  4. show that even a working logit mask is biased, because this model does not renormalise its top-k weights;
  5. measure what routing depends on (domain, language, paraphrase), each against a control;
  6. handle the padded-batch trap, which has an MoE-specific twist: the router's output has no batch axis;
  7. see how far a single generic script gets across other MoE families.

Our model is allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0924: 6.9B total parameters, 1.3B active, 16 layers, 64 experts per layer, top-8 routing. It is small enough to run on CPU, which is what we do here — it needs about 14 GB of RAM in bfloat16 and no GPU at all.

We load the model on CPU in bfloat16. Two loading notes worth knowing before you copy this line:

  • Use device="cpu", not device_map="cpu" — the latter is currently ignored and the model lands on cuda:0.
  • Do not reach for dtype="nf4" to shrink an MoE. On transformers 5 the experts are stored as 3-D nn.Parameter stacks rather than nn.Linear layers, and bitsandbytes only swaps nn.Linear. On this model that quantises the 64 attention projections and none of the 6.4B parameters of expert weights — measured at 12.53 GiB against 12.89 GiB for bfloat16. Worse for us, it would perturb the router's input while leaving the router exact, which is the one confound a routing study cannot afford.

    dtype="bfloat16",
    device="cpu",
    dispatch=True,
)
clear_output()
print(model)

segments.html:
1. Finding the router

The printout above ends each layer with an OlmoeSparseMoeBlock instead of the usual MLP. Let's look at one on its own.

segments.code:
cfg = model.config
E, K = cfg.num_experts, cfg.num_experts_per_tok
N_LAYERS = cfg.num_hidden_layers
print(f"{N_LAYERS} layers, {E} experts per layer, top-{K} routing")

LAYER = 8
mlp = model.model.layers[LAYER].mlp
gate = mlp.gate

print(mlp)

segments.text:
16 layers, 64 experts per layer, top-8 routing
OlmoeSparseMoeBlock(
  (gate): OlmoeTopKRouter()
  (experts): OlmoeExperts(
    (act_fn): SiLUActivation()
  )
)

segments.html: Two children: a gate (the router) and an experts module. Note what is not there — there is no experts[0], experts[1], ... to hook. OlmoeExperts keeps all 64 experts in two 3-D parameter stacks and loops over slices of them, so an individual expert is not an nn.Module and has no envoy of its own.

segments.code:
for name, p in mlp._module.named_parameters():
    print(f"{name:28s} {tuple(p.shape)}  {p.dtype}")

segments.text:
gate.weight                  (64, 2048)  torch.bfloat16
experts.gate_up_proj         (64, 2048, 2048)  torch.bfloat16
experts.down_proj            (64, 2048, 1024)  torch.bfloat16

segments.html:
So the router is a 2048 -> 64 projection and every expert lives inside those two (64, ...) stacks. That tells us where the routing decision is made, but not what the module returns. Rather than guess, we can print the module's forward with .source, which renders the actual Python of forward with a label for every traceable operation inside it. This works without weights loaded, so you can do it before committing to a 14 GB download.

Start with the parent, not the router. .source is usually introduced as a way to reach values inside a forward, but it is just as useful for the opposite question: what does the caller do with a child's return value?

segments.code: print(mlp.source)

segments.text:
* def forward(self, hidden_states: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
                          0     batch_size, sequence_length, hidden_dim = hidden_states.shape
 hidden_states_view_0 ->  1     hidden_states = hidden_states.view(-1, hidden_dim)
 self_gate_0          ->  2     _, top_k_weights, top_k_index = self.gate(hidden_states)
 self_experts_0       ->  3     final_hidden_states = self.experts(hidden_states, top_k_index, top_k_weights).reshape(
 reshape_0            ->  +     ...
                          4         batch_size, sequence_length, hidden_dim
                          5     )
                          6     return final_hidden_states
                          7

segments.html: Line 2 is the whole story:

segments.code: _, top_k_weights, top_k_index = self.gate(hidden_states)

segments.html:
The router returns three things, and the block throws the first one away. Keep that _ in mind — it is the entire subject of section 3.

Line 1 matters too: hidden_states.view(-1, hidden_dim) flattens batch and sequence together before the router is called, so everything the router sees and returns is indexed (batch * seq, ...). That is section 6.

Now the router's own forward.

segments.code: print(gate.source)

segments.text:
* def forward(self, hidden_states):
 hidden_states_reshape_0       ->  0     hidden_states = hidden_states.reshape(-1, self.hidden_dim)
 F_linear_0                    ->  1     router_logits = F.linear(hidden_states, self.weight)  # (seq_len, num_experts)
 torch_nn_functional_softmax_0 ->  2     router_probs = torch.nn.functional.softmax(router_logits, dtype=torch.float, dim=-1)
 torch_topk_0                  ->  3     router_top_value, router_indices = torch.topk(router_probs, self.top_k, dim=-1)  # (seq_len, top_k)
                                   4     if self.norm_topk_prob:
 router_top_value_sum_0        ->  5         router_top_value /= router_top_value.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
 router_top_value_to_0         ->  6     router_top_value = router_top_value.to(router_logits.dtype)
                                   7     router_scores = router_top_value
                                   8     return router_logits, router_scores, router_indices
                                   9

segments.html:
OlmoeTopKRouter.forward is six lines: a linear projection to router_logits, a softmax over all 64 experts, a topk, an optional renormalisation guarded by self.norm_topk_prob, and a return of (router_logits, router_scores, router_indices).

That is everything we need, and none of it requires .source to read — the three values are the module's ordinary output. Let's take them.

segments.code:
prompt = "The capital of France is Paris and the capital of Germany is"

with torch.no_grad():
    with model.trace(prompt):
        router_in = gate.input.save()                # .input BEFORE .output!
        router_logits, routing_weights, expert_idx = gate.output
        router_logits   = router_logits.save()
        routing_weights = routing_weights.save()
        expert_idx      = expert_idx.save()

print("gate.input          ", tuple(router_in.shape),       router_in.dtype)
print("gate.output[0] logits ", tuple(router_logits.shape),   router_logits.dtype)
print("gate.output[1] weights", tuple(routing_weights.shape), routing_weights.dtype)
print("gate.output[2] indices", tuple(expert_idx.shape),      expert_idx.dtype)
print()
n_tokens = len(model.tokenizer(prompt)["input_ids"])
print(f"the prompt is {n_tokens} tokens long")

segments.text:
gate.input           (12, 2048) torch.bfloat16
gate.output[0] logits  (12, 64) torch.bfloat16
gate.output[1] weights (12, 8) torch.bfloat16
gate.output[2] indices (12, 8) torch.int64

the prompt is 12 tokens long

segments.html:
Two things to notice.

First, the shapes are (T, E), (T, K), (T, K) — there is no batch axis. A 12-token prompt gives (12, 64), not (1, 12, 64), because of that view(-1, hidden_dim) in the parent. With one sequence this is harmless; with a padded batch it is not, and section 6 shows what goes wrong.

Second, we asked for gate.input before gate.output. .input and .output of the same module are two ordered events in the forward pass, and requesting them out of order raises OutOfOrderError naming the exact value. The same rule bites later: read mlp.gate.output before mlp.output, since the router runs first.

We can also see the routing decision for one token directly.

segments.code:
tokens = [model.tokenizer.decode(t) for t in model.tokenizer(prompt)["input_ids"]]
print(f"routing for the final token {tokens[-1]!r}:")
order = routing_weights[-1].float().argsort(descending=True)
for rank, slot in enumerate(order.tolist()):
    e = int(expert_idx[-1][slot])
    print(f"   rank {rank}: expert {e:2d}   weight {routing_weights[-1][slot].item():.4f}"
          f"   logit {router_logits[-1][e].item():+.3f}")
print(f"   these {K} weights sum to {routing_weights[-1].float().sum():.4f}")

segments.html:
2. Anchoring the wiring

We now have three tensors that look like a routing decision. Before we build any statistics on them we should check that they are wired together the way we think, because a plausible-looking tensor read from the wrong place produces plausible-looking science. Two claims are worth testing, and both are one line:

Anchor A — the experts in gate.output[2] are the top-8 of the logits in gate.output[0].

Anchor B — the weights in gate.output[1] are the softmax of those logits, gathered at those indices.

segments.code:
probs = torch.softmax(router_logits.float(), dim=-1)
my_idx = probs.topk(K, dim=-1).indices

print("A: topk(softmax(logits)) == gate.output[2], exactly and in rank order :",
      torch.equal(my_idx, expert_idx))

gathered = probs.gather(-1, expert_idx)
err = (routing_weights.float() - gathered).abs().max().item()
print(f"B: max|weights - softmax(logits)[idx]| = {err:.3e}")
print(f"   (full 64-way softmax row sums: {probs.sum(-1).min():.6f} .. {probs.sum(-1).max():.6f})")

segments.text:
A: topk(softmax(logits)) == gate.output[2], exactly and in rank order : True
B: max|weights - softmax(logits)[idx]| = 8.268e-04
   (full 64-way softmax row sums: 1.000000 .. 1.000000)

segments.html:
Anchor A passes exactly — not just as a set, but in the same rank order. Anchor B passes to 8e-4, which is the resolution of bfloat16 around weights of order 0.05: the router computes its softmax in float32 and casts the result back down on the way out (router_top_value.to(router_logits.dtype), line 6 of the source above), so this is rounding, not a wiring error. Load the model in float32 and the residual shrinks accordingly.

Now a third check that is not a wiring test but a configuration test, and which turns out to matter more than either of the above.

segments.code:
mass = routing_weights.float().sum(-1)
print(f"B': top-{K} routing weights sum to {mass.mean():.4f} on average "
      f"(min {mass.min():.4f}, max {mass.max():.4f})")
print(f"    config.norm_topk_prob = {cfg.norm_topk_prob}")

renormalised = gathered / gathered.sum(-1, keepdim=True)
print(f"    max|weights - RENORMALISED softmax| = "
      f"{(routing_weights.float() - renormalised).abs().max():.3f}")

segments.text:
B': top-8 routing weights sum to 0.4412 on average (min 0.3254, max 0.7766)
    config.norm_topk_prob = False
    max|weights - RENORMALISED softmax| = 0.190

segments.html:
The top-8 weights do not sum to 1. Because norm_topk_prob=False, this model uses the raw 64-way softmax probabilities as its mixing weights, so the eight chosen experts carry only about 44% of the probability mass and the MoE block's output is scaled down accordingly. Many MoE models (Mixtral, Qwen3-MoE, GPT-OSS) set this to True and their weights sum to 1.0; this one does not.

That is a two-line config detail, and it is the reason the second ablation trap in section 4 exists. Check norm_topk_prob before you ablate anything.

One more anchor, cheap and worth having: recompute the logits ourselves from the router's input and weight matrix.

segments.code:
W = gate.weight                                     # (E, hidden)
recomputed = F.linear(router_in.float(), W.float())
print(f"C: max|W @ h - gate.output[0]| = "
      f"{(recomputed - router_logits.float()).abs().max():.3e}"
      f"   (logit std = {router_logits.float().std():.3f})")

segments.text: C: max|W @ h - gate.output[0]| = 9.927e-03   (logit std = 1.031)

segments.html:
Consistent with bfloat16 output rounding on logits whose spread is about 1.0. The router is a plain linear map of the pre-MoE hidden state, and we are reading the right tensor.

3. Ablating an expert: the trap

The natural causal experiment is: remove one expert, see what breaks. And the natural way to remove an expert from a top-k router is to set its logit to -inf so it can never be picked. nnsight's own vLLM documentation says exactly this — "To ablate an expert, mask its router logit to -inf in mlp.gate.output" — and on vLLM it is correct, because there mlp.gate is a ReplicatedLinear whose output is the logits the block consumes.

On TransformersModel it does nothing at all. Let's not ablate one expert; let's set all 64 logits to -inf and watch the model not care.

segments.code:
with torch.no_grad():
    with model.trace(prompt):
        _, _, base_idx = gate.output
        base_idx  = base_idx.save()
        base_mlp  = mlp.output.save()
        base_lgts = model.output.logits.save()

with torch.no_grad():
    with model.trace(prompt):
        gate.output[0][:, :] = -float("inf")        # every logit, every token
        noop_mlp  = mlp.output.save()
        noop_lgts = model.output.logits.save()

print(f"max|delta| on the MoE block output : {(noop_mlp  - base_mlp ).abs().max():.6f}")
print(f"max|delta| on the model's logits   : {(noop_lgts - base_lgts).abs().max():.6f}")

segments.text:
max|delta| on the MoE block output : 0.000000
max|delta| on the model's logits   : 0.000000

segments.html:
Every router logit in layer 8 is negative infinity and nothing moved. No exception, no warning, no clue.

The reason is the line we read in section 1:

segments.code: _, top_k_weights, top_k_index = self.gate(hidden_states)

segments.html:
Element [0] of the router's return is a vestigial value that the block discards. nnsight did exactly what it promises — it handed us the live tensor and our write landed on it — but no downstream operation ever reads that tensor again.

This is the most dangerous failure mode in intervention work, because it does not look like a failure. Had we skipped this check and gone straight to "ablate expert 18 and measure the loss", we would have reported that expert 18 does not matter, with a clean zero to prove it, and been wrong about all 64 experts.

The general rule: an intervention that lands on a value the caller discards is indistinguishable from an intervention that had no effect. Before trusting an ablation, read the parent's .source and confirm the value you are writing is one the caller actually consumes.

Three sites in this block are consumed. Two are the other elements of the router's output — the weights [1] and the indices [2]. The third is the pre-softmax logits inside the router's forward, which we can reach with .source at the F_linear_0 operation we saw earlier. Let's compare all of them on the same target.

segments.code:
TARGET = int(base_idx[-1, 0])           # the top-ranked expert at the last token
print(f"target expert: {TARGET}\n")

def delta(mlp_out, logits, label):
    print(f"{label:52s} d_mlp {(mlp_out[0, -1] - base_mlp[0, -1]).float().norm():.4f}"
          f"   d_logits {(logits - base_lgts).float().norm():7.2f}")

# (a) the vLLM recipe: mask the returned logits
with torch.no_grad():
    with model.trace(prompt):
        gate.output[0][:, TARGET] = -float("inf")
        m = mlp.output.save(); l = model.output.logits.save()
delta(m, l, "(a) gate.output[0]  logit  <- -inf")

# (b) zero the routing weight wherever this expert was selected
with torch.no_grad():
    with model.trace(prompt):
        _, w, i = gate.output
        w[i == TARGET] = 0.0
        m = mlp.output.save(); l = model.output.logits.save()
delta(m, l, "(b) gate.output[1]  weight <- 0")

# (c) selection ablation: re-run the top-k with this expert excluded,
#     but gather the weights from the UNTOUCHED softmax
with torch.no_grad():
    with model.trace(prompt):
        lo, w, i = gate.output
        p = torch.softmax(lo.float(), dim=-1)
        p_masked = p.clone()
        p_masked[:, TARGET] = -1.0
        new_i = p_masked.topk(K, dim=-1).indices
        new_w = p.gather(-1, new_i).to(w.dtype)
        hit = (i == TARGET).any(-1, keepdim=True)     # touch only affected tokens
        gate.output = (lo, torch.where(hit, new_w, w), torch.where(hit, new_i, i))
        m = mlp.output.save(); l = model.output.logits.save()
delta(m, l, "(c) gate.output = (logits, new weights, new indices)")

# (d) mask the logit inside the router, before the softmax
with torch.no_grad():
    with model.trace(prompt):                       # warm-up trace for .source
        pass
with torch.no_grad():
    with model.trace(prompt):
        gate.source.F_linear_0.output[:, TARGET] = -float("inf")
        m = mlp.output.save(); l = model.output.logits.save()
delta(m, l, "(d) gate.source.F_linear_0.output <- -inf")

# reference: delete the whole MoE block
with torch.no_grad():
    with model.trace(prompt):
        mlp.output[:] = 0.0
        m = mlp.output.save(); l = model.output.logits.save()
delta(m, l, "    (reference) zero the entire MoE block")

(a) gate.output[0]  logit  <- -inf                   d_mlp 0.0000   d_logits    0.00
(b) gate.output[1]  weight <- 0                      d_mlp 0.1687   d_logits  125.58
(c) gate.output = (logits, new weights, new indices) d_mlp 0.1715   d_logits  125.28
(d) gate.source.F_linear_0.output <- -inf            d_mlp 0.1706   d_logits  123.77
(reference) zero the entire MoE block            d_mlp 0.3133   d_logits  876.74

segments.html:
Sites (b), (c) and (d) all move the model; site (a) is flat zero. Note that the .source intervention in (d) needed a throwaway trace first — the first .source access on a module raises OutOfOrderError when the block has already read something from it, once per module, and a warm-up trace clears it.

(b), (c) and (d) land within a couple of percent of each other on this prompt, but they are not the same experiment, and section 4 shows where they come apart. They are three different counterfactuals:

  • (b) zero the weight. The expert's contribution is removed and nothing replaces it, so the block's total mixing mass drops from ~0.44 to ~0.44 − w.
  • (c) selection ablation. The expert is removed from the shortlist and the 9th-ranked expert takes its slot, with the weight it would have had. Mixing mass stays where it was. This is "what would this layer have done with 63 experts".
  • (d) mask the logit pre-softmax. Same selection change as (c) — plus the softmax denominator shrinks, so every surviving weight gets slightly larger.

Which one is right depends on the question, but only one of them survives the control in the next section.

4. The second trap: which ablation is honest?

Any expert-ablation study needs a null. The cleanest one available is: an expert that no token in the corpus routes to must produce exactly zero change. If a method reports a nonzero effect for an expert the model never uses, then whatever number it reports for a real expert includes that much fiction.

We run each of the three working ablations on four experts at layer 8 — the most used, the median, the rarest that is used at all, and one that is never selected — over a short prose corpus. The effect size is the mean KL divergence between the original and ablated next-token distributions, which is zero if and only if nothing changed.

segments.code:
PROSE_ABL = "\n\n".join([
    "The harbour at Bergen has been in continuous use since the eleventh century, when merchants "
    "from the Hanseatic League established a trading post on the eastern shore. Timber, dried cod and "
    "iron ore moved south through the fjords, while grain and cloth arrived from the Baltic ports. The "
    "wooden warehouses that line the quay were rebuilt many times after fires, most recently in the "
    "eighteenth century, and they now house museums and small restaurants rather than cargo.",

    "Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in carbohydrates. In plants the "
    "reaction takes place inside chloroplasts, organelles that contain stacked membranes called "
    "thylakoids. Chlorophyll molecules embedded in those membranes absorb photons, chiefly in the blue "
    "and red parts of the spectrum, and transfer the excitation to a reaction centre where water is "
    "split and oxygen is released as a by-product.",

    "The trial of Galileo before the Roman Inquisition in 1633 turned less on astronomy than on "
    "authority. Galileo had published a dialogue in which the Copernican account of the heavens was "
    "defended by the more persuasive of two speakers, and the church held that he had violated an "
    "earlier injunction. He was compelled to abjure, and spent the remainder of his life under house "
    "arrest at Arcetri.",
])

abl_ids = model.tokenizer(PROSE_ABL, return_tensors="pt")["input_ids"]
print("corpus:", abl_ids.shape[1], "tokens")

with torch.no_grad():
    with model.trace(abl_ids):
        _, _, corpus_idx = gate.output
        corpus_idx = corpus_idx.save()
        corpus_lgts = model.output.logits.save()

base_logp = F.log_softmax(corpus_lgts[0].float(), dim=-1)

def mean_kl(new_logits):
    lp = F.log_softmax(new_logits[0].float(), dim=-1)
    return float((base_logp.exp() * (base_logp - lp)).sum(-1).mean())

counts = torch.bincount(corpus_idx.reshape(-1), minlength=E)

segments.code:
def ablate_expert(target, method):
    with torch.no_grad():
        with model.trace(abl_ids):
            if method == "logit":                    # mask pre-softmax, via .source
                gate.source.F_linear_0.output[:, target] = -float("inf")
            else:
                lo, w, i = gate.output
                if method == "weight":               # zero the weight
                    w[i == target] = 0.0
                else:                                # selection ablation
                    p = torch.softmax(lo.float(), dim=-1)
                    pm = p.clone()
                    pm[:, target] = -1.0
                    ni = pm.topk(K, dim=-1).indices
                    nw = p.gather(-1, ni).to(w.dtype)
                    hit = (i == target).any(-1, keepdim=True)
                    gate.output = (lo, torch.where(hit, nw, w),
                                       torch.where(hit, ni, i))
            out = model.output.logits.save()
    return mean_kl(out)

picks = [("most used",      int(order[0])),
         ("median",         int(order[E // 2])),
         (f"rarest ({rarest_n} sel)", [j for j in range(E) if counts[j] == rarest_n][0]),
         ("NEVER selected", int(order[-1]))]

with torch.no_grad():
    with model.trace(abl_ids[:, :4]):                # warm up .source
        pass

print(f"{'expert':22s} {'id':>4s} {'sel':>5s} {'logit mask':>12s} {'weight->0':>12s} {'selection':>12s}")
for label, e in picks:
    row = [ablate_expert(e, m) for m in ("logit", "weight", "selection")]
    print(f"{label:22s} {e:4d} {int(counts[e]):5d} " + " ".join(f"{v:12.6f}" for v in row))

with torch.no_grad():

segments.html:
Read the bottom row of the table first. Zeroing the weight and ablating the selection both give exactly 0.000000 for an expert that no token routes to. They pass the null.

Masking the logit does not. It reports 0.00038 for expert 27, which the model never once selects. That is not a small error in absolute terms — it is more than twice the real effect of the rarest expert that is used (0.00016), and about a third of the median expert's. An expert-importance ranking built from logit masks is noise in its entire lower half.

The cause is norm_topk_prob=False from section 2. Because the routing weights are raw softmax probabilities, removing one expert from the softmax shrinks the denominator and inflates every surviving weight, whether or not the removed expert was ever in the top-8. The whole MoE block simply gets slightly louder.

For scale, note the last line of the table: deleting the whole MoE block costs 0.070, and the single most-used expert accounts for 0.0082 of that — 12% of the block's causal contribution from 5% of its routing slots. Slightly super-proportional, but nothing like a bottleneck. No one expert of the 64 is load-bearing at this layer.

segments.html:
A 1.1% uniform gain on the MoE block, applied at every token, purely from deleting an expert that was never used. That is the whole spurious signal — and it is a systematic one, not noise: it is larger for experts that hold more softmax mass, which correlates with how often they are selected, so it inflates exactly the numbers you were hoping to compare.

The rule: ablate by selection, not by logit — recompute the top-k with the expert excluded, and gather the weights from the untouched softmax. Then verify with a never-selected expert, which must give exactly zero.

Zeroing the weight passes the null too, and it is a legitimate experiment; it just answers a different question. It removes the expert's contribution without letting the router replace it, so it measures "how much did this expert contribute" rather than "what would this layer do without it". Report which one you ran.

(If your model sets norm_topk_prob=True, the logit mask is much better behaved, because the renormalisation cancels the denominator change for the surviving experts. It is still worth running the null.)

A footnote on that hit guard

The selection ablation above contains one line whose purpose is not obvious:

segments.code:
hit = (i == target).any(-1, keepdim=True)
gate.output = (lo, torch.where(hit, nw, w), torch.where(hit, ni, i))

segments.html: We rebuild the top-k for every token but only install it where the target expert was actually selected. That looks redundant — for a token that never picked the expert, our recomputed top-k should equal the model's. It very nearly does, and "very nearly" is enough to break the control.

segments.code:
with torch.no_grad():
    with model.trace(abl_ids):
        lo, w, i = gate.output
        p = torch.softmax(lo.float(), dim=-1)
        pm = p.clone()
        pm[:, never_e] = -1.0
        ni = pm.topk(K, dim=-1).indices
        set_differs = (ni.sort(-1).values != i.sort(-1).values).any(-1).sum().save()
        order_differs = (ni != i).sum().save()
        nw = p.gather(-1, ni).to(w.dtype)
        weight_err = (nw.float() - w.float()).abs().max().save()

print(f"recomputing the top-{K} with a NEVER-selected expert masked out, "
      f"{abl_ids.shape[1]} tokens:")
print(f"  tokens whose selected SET changed  : {int(set_differs)}")
print(f"  slots whose rank ORDER changed     : {int(order_differs)}")
print(f"  max |our weights - model weights|  : {float(weight_err):.3e}")

recomputing the top-8 with a NEVER-selected expert masked out, 259 tokens:
  tokens whose selected SET changed  : 3

segments.html:
Three tokens out of 259 come back with a different set of experts, even though the expert we masked was never in any of them. Our softmax and the model's are not bit-identical — F.softmax(x, dtype=torch.float) and torch.softmax(x.float()) can disagree in the last bit — and on those tokens the 8th and 9th experts are close enough that the last bit decides. Reordering within the top-k is harmless (the same experts get the same weights), but a changed set is a real intervention on a token we did not mean to touch, and it leaks straight into the never-selected control. Without the guard the control reports a nonzero effect and the whole point of the null is lost.

The general lesson is the same one as section 3, from the other side: when you replace a value the model computed, replace only the part you mean to change, and derive everything else from the model's own tensors rather than from your reimplementation of them.

5. What does routing actually depend on?

With reading anchored and ablation understood, we can ask the descriptive question: do different kinds of text use different experts?

We need a corpus with several clearly different domains. We write it out inline so nothing depends on a downloaded dataset: English encyclopaedic prose, source code, and the same kind of prose in French and German.

segments.html:
Now a capture function. We want the expert indices at every layer for every token, which is one trace per sequence with 16 saves in it.

Two idioms are worth pointing out. First, we wrap the whole thing in torch.no_grad() — a read-only trace otherwise runs with autograd on, which costs roughly 18x the memory for nothing. Second, a list comprehension of .save() calls bound to a local name inside the trace body does not survive the block; use nnsight.save([...]) on the whole list instead.

One deliberate omission: normally you would put these sequences into a single trace with several tracer.invoke calls, which runs them in one forward instead of fifteen and is one of the clearest wins nnsight offers over raw hooks. We do not, because our sequences have different lengths and batching them means padding them — and for this statistic padding is exactly the thing that goes wrong. Section 6 shows what it costs and how to batch safely once you know.

The four rows are visibly different. Code concentrates hard on a few experts that English prose barely uses; the French and German rows look more like each other than like English. But "visibly different" is not a number, and with 64 bins and a few hundred tokens per group, two samples of the same distribution would also look somewhat different.

So we quantify the difference with the Jensen-Shannon divergence between usage histograms (in bits, 0 = identical, 1 = disjoint), and — this is the part that matters — we give it a control: the JS divergence between two random halves of the same group, at the same sample size. segments.html:
Three things to read off this plot.

Code is the strongest signal and it grows with depth. It starts at 0.17 in layer 0 — already well above the noise floor, but the smallest it ever gets — and climbs steadily to 0.59 by layer 15, averaging 0.43 against a control of 0.011. That is roughly 40x the divergence sampling noise produces. Early layers route partly on surface form, which code and prose partly share; the separation is built up through the stack.

English versus French or German is a late-layer effect. Those curves sit low and flat through the middle of the network (0.09 to 0.20) and then jump sharply at the last layer, to 0.49 and 0.57. Whatever the final-layer experts are doing, "is this English" is a large part of it, and it is not something the middle of the network routes on.

French and German route almost identically to each other: 0.041 on average, only about 4x the control, and the flattest curve on the plot. The model separates English from not-English far more sharply than it separates one non-English language from another.

The control line is why any of this is believable. Two random halves of the same corpus, at the same sample size, give 0.011 at every layer. That is the floor. The code signal is 40x it and unmistakable; the French-German difference is 4x it and should be treated as suggestive at this sample size — which is precisely the calibration a control exists to provide.

We can also ask how concentrated routing is, rather than how different — the entropy of the usage histogram, in bits, against a ceiling of log2(64) = 6.

Code does not just use different experts, it uses fewer of them, and it does so from layer 4 onward: its usage entropy sits about a full bit below English prose's for most of the stack, which is an effective repertoire of roughly 23 experts against prose's 48.

French and German concentrate too, but only at the very last layer — consistent with the divergence plot, where their separation from English is also a last-layer event. English prose is the only group whose routing stays broad all the way up.

5b. Is routing stable under paraphrase?

Usage histograms are a property of a corpus. A sharper question is whether the routing of a single token position tracks meaning: do four different surface forms of the same proposition select the same experts?

We take four groups of four paraphrases each, look at the final token (a full stop in every sentence, so the token itself is matched), and measure the Jaccard overlap of the top-8 expert sets. Two controls come along for free:

  • cross-group pairs — a paraphrase of proposition A against a paraphrase of proposition B. These are the same kind of sentence, so this controls for "being a short declarative fact".
  • unrelated sentences, also ending in a full stop.

Chance overlap for two random 8-of-64 sets is about 0.067.

def jaccard(a, b):
    sa, sb = set(a.tolist()), set(b.tolist())
    return len(sa & sb) / len(sa | sb)

Paraphrases of the same proposition route to substantially the same experts — mean Jaccard 0.80 against 0.55 for unrelated sentences — and the gap opens up with depth. From layer 12 onward the paraphrase curve climbs while both controls fall away, and by layer 15 four different surface forms of one fact select 7.8 of the same 8 experts (0.972) where unrelated sentences ending in the same token share about half.

The cross-group control is what makes this a statement about meaning rather than about style. Those sentences are the same length, register and syntax as the within-group pairs and differ only in which proposition they express — and they track the unrelated baseline, not the paraphrase line.

Two honest caveats the plot makes visible. In the early and middle layers all three curves sit close together and wander (layers 7 and 10 push every curve up together), so the separation is genuinely a late-stack phenomenon and the middle of the plot is mostly sample noise on 24 pairs. And every curve is far above the 0.067 chance line everywhere, including the unrelated one: any two tokens in this model share several experts simply because some experts are used much more than others. It is the difference between the curves that carries the signal, not their height.

6. The padding trap

Everything so far ran one sequence at a time. Batching is normally the right thing to do, and it is where nnsight's tracer.invoke shines — but MoE routing statistics over a padded batch have a trap that is easy to miss and impossible to see in the shapes.

Recall from section 1 that the block flattens batch and sequence together before calling the router. So gate.output[0] is (B*T, E). A single 7-token sequence gives (7, 64); three sequences padded to length 16 give (48, 64). Both are 2-D, both index tokens on axis 0, and nothing in the tensor marks where one sequence ends and the next begins. Any code that averages over gate.output[0] therefore averages over pad rows too, silently.

    ref.append(entropy(gl.float().softmax(-1)))
print("batch-1 shapes:", [tuple(r.shape) for r in ref])
reference = torch.cat(ref).mean()

enc = tk(texts, return_tensors="pt", padding=True)

print(f"MASKED mean over attention_mask == 1   = {masked:.6f}")

segments.html:
The masked statistic matches the unpadded reference to the digit; the naive one does not.

Note why it does not: pad rows are not inert. They are real hidden states that get routed to real experts, and their routing entropy is higher than that of real tokens — the router has no strong opinion about a padding token, so it spreads its mass. That biases mean entropy upward and pollutes any expert-usage histogram in a direction that depends only on how much padding you happened to have.

The fix is two lines: reshape (B*T, ...) back to (B, T, ...), then index by attention_mask. The trap is that nothing forces you to, and the numbers you get without it look perfectly reasonable.

7. How far does one script get?

Everything above used exactly one model path: model.model.layers[L].mlp.gate, whose .output is a 3-tuple. How much of that is OLMoE-specific?

transformers 5 standardised MoE routing into a *Router / *TopKRouter module, so a generic finder — look for a module whose class name contains "router", or a child named gate/router under something MoE-ish — reaches the routing decision on most families with no per-family code at all. We can test that on tiny randomly-initialised models, which download in seconds. Their weights are random, so nothing here is a scientific result — this is purely a wiring survey.

segments.code:
import gc

def find_router(m):
    for name, env in m.named_modules():
        cls = type(env._module).__name__.lower()
        leaf = name.split(".")[-1].lower()
        near_moe = any(k in name.lower()
                       for k in ("moe", "mlp", "block_sparse", "feed_forward", "ffn"))
        if "router" in cls or (leaf in ("gate", "router", "wg") and near_moe):
            return name, env
    return None, None

def describe(x):
    if isinstance(x, torch.Tensor):
        return f"T{tuple(x.shape)}"
    if isinstance(x, (tuple, list)):
        return "(" + ", ".join(describe(e) for e in x) + ")"
    return type(x).__name__

def tensors(x):
    if isinstance(x, torch.Tensor):
        return [x]
    if isinstance(x, (tuple, list)):
        return [t for e in x for t in tensors(e)]
    return []

REPOS = ["yujiepan/qwen3-moe-tiny-random", "yujiepan/qwen3.5-moe-tiny-random",
         "yujiepan/qwen3-next-moe-tiny-random", "yujiepan/gpt-oss-tiny-random-bf16",
         "yujiepan/mixtral-8xtiny-random", "yujiepan/glm-4-moe-tiny-random",
         "yujiepan/glm-4-moe-lite-tiny-random", "yujiepan/ernie-4.5-moe-tiny-random",
         "yujiepan/gemma-4-moe-tiny-random", "yujiepan/jamba-tiny-random",
         "yujiepan/olmo-3-tiny-random",                       # dense: no router at all
         "yujiepan/deepseek-v3-tiny-random", "yujiepan/dbrx-tiny-random",
         "yujiepan/llama-4-tiny-random"]

SWEEP_PROMPT = "The capital of France is Paris and the capital of Germany is"
rows = []
for repo in REPOS:
    short = (repo.split("/")[-1].replace("-tiny-random", "")
             .replace("tiny-random", "").replace("--", "-").strip("-"))
    row = {"repo": short}
    try:
        m = TransformersModel(repo, task="text-generation", device="cpu",
                              dispatch=True, trust_remote_code=True)
        c = getattr(m.config, "text_config", m.config)
        ne = (getattr(c, "num_experts", None) or getattr(c, "num_local_experts", None)
              or getattr(c, "n_routed_experts", None))
        kk = getattr(c, "num_experts_per_tok", None) or getattr(c, "moe_topk", None)
        if isinstance(kk, list):
            kk = kk[0]
        path, env = find_router(m)
        if path is None:
            row["verdict"] = "no router (dense model)"
        else:
            with torch.no_grad():
                with m.trace(SWEEP_PROMPT):
                    out = env.output.save()
            cut = path.find("layers.")
            row["path"] = ("..." + path[cut:]) if cut > 0 else path
            row["output"] = describe(out)
            ts = tensors(out)
            lg = [t for t in ts if t.is_floating_point() and t.shape[-1] == ne]
            ix = [t for t in ts if not t.is_floating_point() and t.shape[-1] == kk]
            wt = [t for t in ts if t.is_floating_point() and t.shape[-1] == kk]
            if lg and ix:
                Lg = lg[0].float().reshape(-1, ne)
                I = ix[0].reshape(-1, kk)
                ok = bool((Lg.topk(kk, -1).indices.sort(-1).values
                           == I.sort(-1).values).all())
                row["topk==logits"] = ok
                if wt:
                    Wt = wt[0].float().reshape(-1, kk)
                    row["weight sum"] = round(float(Wt.sum(-1).mean()), 3)
                row["verdict"] = "generic anchor OK" if ok else "reached, anchor FAILS"
            else:
                row["verdict"] = "reached, anchor n/a"
        del m
        gc.collect()
    except Exception as e:
        row["verdict"] = f"did not load: {type(e).__name__}"
    rows.append(row)
    clear_output(wait=True)
    print(f"{len(rows)}/{len(REPOS)} ...")

clear_output()
hdr = f"{'model':18s} {'router path':34s} {'router .output':40s} {'wsum':>6s}  verdict"
print(hdr); print("-" * len(hdr))
for r in rows:
    print(f"{r['repo']:18s} {r.get('path', '-'):34s} {r.get('output', '-'):40s} "
          f"{str(r.get('weight sum', '-')):>6s}  {r['verdict']}")

segments.html:
Read the table in three parts.

Where the numbers live is now uniform. Every MoE family that loads exposes its routing decision at a *Router module under the MLP, and all but one return (logits, weights, indices) with the shapes we saw on OLMoE. One generic finder, no per-family code, no .source. The dense control (olmo-3) correctly finds nothing, so the heuristic is not hallucinating routers.

What the numbers mean is not uniform. Look at the weight-sum column and the anchor verdicts:

  • Models with norm_topk_prob=True sum to 1.0; OLMoE sums to 0.44; glm-4-moe sums to 2.5, because it applies a routed_scaling_factor after normalising.
  • ernie-4.5-moe and glm-4-moe-lite fail the generic anchor: their selected experts are not the top-k of a softmax over the logits. These are DeepSeek-style routers, which score with a sigmoid, add a learned per-expert bias for load balancing, and restrict the choice to a few expert groups. The logits you read are real, but topk(softmax(logits)) is not the selection rule, and a script that assumes it will quietly mis-attribute every token.
  • jamba returns a bare tensor of logits, not a tuple. Its router was never refactored, so you do the softmax and the top-k yourself.

Some families do not load at all, for reasons that have nothing to do with tracing: deepseek-v3's remote code is written against transformers 4.x, and dbrx and llama-4 trip their own config validators. Every one of these reproduces with a plain model(**inputs) and no nnsight anywhere. If a sweep like this fails, run the plain forward before blaming the tracer — the traceback of a failure inside the model surfaces at your with model.trace(...) line, which makes it very easy to misattribute.

So the practical answer: reading routing generalises; interpreting it does not. Write the reader once, and write a per-family logits -> selection rule.

Limitations

  • One model, one size. All the science here is OLMoE-1B-7B. Its 64-expert, top-8, un-renormalised router is one point in a large design space, and the numbers — especially the sizes of the divergences — are not portable. The method is; the values are not.
  • Small corpora. A few hundred tokens per domain and 24 paraphrase pairs. The split-half and cross-group controls are there precisely because the samples are small, and they bound how much of each effect could be noise, but wider claims need more text.
  • Usage histograms are not specialisation. "Code uses a different set of experts than prose" is a statement about correlation between input type and routing. It does not show that those experts compute anything code-specific; for that you would need to ablate them on code and on prose and compare, which is a study of its own.
  • One layer of causal work. The ablation section only measured layer 8. Expert importance almost certainly varies with depth, and the layer-8 result (the most-used expert of 64 carries an effect a small fraction of the whole block's) should not be assumed to hold at layer 0 or 15.
  • bfloat16 on CPU. Anchor B is 8e-4 rather than exactly zero because of it, and the tiny ablation effects are measured through the same rounding. Nothing here turns on a difference that small, but a study that did should run in float32.
  • Ablation is not the only causal tool. Removing an expert answers "what happens without it". It does not tell you what the expert does; expert steering (forcing a token to a chosen expert) and attribution methods answer different and often better questions.

Next steps

  • Activation patching for localising behaviour rather than deleting capacity.
  • The .source guide for reaching values inside a forward, which is what made intervention (d) possible.
  • The vLLM backend if you need to run a large MoE at speed — but note that the expert-ablation recipe there is vLLM-specific, for the reason section 3 demonstrates.
